title: Shraddha Kapoor Gives Birth Backstage, Then Walks Out to Dance. The 'Eetha' Teaser Is the Boldest She's Ever Been.
excerpt: Maddock Films trades horror-comedy for a thunderous Lavani biopic — and Shraddha's transformation into folk legend Vithabai Narayangaonkar already looks career-defining. In cinemas August 28.
body:
The crowd is restless. Dancers are on stage, the lanterns are swaying, the dholki is going — and still the audience won't stop shouting one name. *"Eetha ko bulao!"* They paid to see her, and they will not be denied. The camera finds her backstage. She is in the middle of giving birth. And she is already reaching for her ghungroos.

That is the opening forty seconds of the **Eetha** teaser, and by the time **Shraddha Kapoor** rises, drapes a blood-red and gold nine-yard saree over a body that has just delivered a child, and walks out into the roar — you understand exactly what kind of film **Maddock Films** has made. Not a horror-comedy. Not a rom-com. A folk epic, drenched in sweat and defiance, about a woman who refused to be ordinary.

> "Padi padi mari toh bechari kehlaungi. Naachte hue mari toh misaal ban jaaungi." — Eetha, in the teaser

If I die helpless, I'll be called a poor soul. If I die dancing, I'll become a legend. It is the kind of line that detonates in a packed theatre — and it did, because the teaser premiered on the big screen alongside **Cocktail 2** before the makers put it online, leaking first and going viral on the strength of one image: Shraddha Kapoor like you have never seen her.

**Eetha** is the screen story of **Vithabai Bhau Mang Narayangaonkar**, the towering Tamasha and Lavani performer who is, genuinely, the stuff of Maharashtrian folklore — the artiste who is said to have given birth backstage and returned to the stage minutes later. It is a real life almost too cinematic to be true, and casting Shraddha against type is the gamble that makes this interesting. For years she has been the soft, luminous lead of the Stree universe, the studio's most bankable scream queen. Here she is all kohl and grit and raw stamina, her face caked in stage paint, her eyes doing the work that dialogue can't. On first look, she's never been better.


The craftsmanship is loud in the best way. Director **Laxman Utekar** and producer **Dinesh Vijan** are reuniting straight off the runaway success of *Chhaava*, and they have poured that goodwill into scale — sprawling village sets, a sea of cheering spectators, costumes by Sheetal Iqbal Sharma that turn every frame into a moving painting. The choreography is by **Vaibhavi Merchant**, which matters enormously in a film where the dance *is* the drama, and the score comes from **Ajay-Atul**, the only composers who could give Lavani both its earthiness and its grandeur. **Randeep Hooda** and Mohammed Zeeshan Ayyub round out the cast in pivotal roles. The whole thing looks expensive and unembarrassed about it.

What the teaser smartly withholds is the cost. You see the adulation, the lanterns, the standing ovations — but the flickers of anguish between the performances suggest the film knows that a woman who lived for the stage paid dearly for it. That tension, between the legend and the person, is what separates a biopic from a highlight reel. We'll see in August whether the screenplay by Kshitij Patwardhan can hold both.

**Eetha** hits theatres on **August 28, 2026**, sliding into a ferociously crowded Raksha Bandhan weekend where it clashes with Sidharth Malhotra's *Vvan* and Yash's *Toxic*, among others — a rare four-way festival pile-up. For the diaspora, this is a Maddock title, which means a confident international theatrical footprint: expect it across major US, UK, Canada and Gulf chains on opening weekend, with the eventual streaming home almost certainly **Netflix**, the studio's usual post-theatrical partner. Subtitles and a Marathi-flavoured Hindi soundtrack should travel well for audiences who grew up on this music even an ocean away.

Bollywood keeps telling us its heroines have nothing left to prove. Then a teaser like this arrives, and a star who built a career on charm walks out, mid-childbirth, to dance for a crowd that won't let her rest — and reminds everyone what a transformation actually looks like.
